strengths: Addresses a genuine and timely gap: existing knowledge editing benchmarks are static and contaminated, and CRAFT's automatically updatable pipeline built on official statistical/financial data sources is a practical contribution to the field

Contamination analysis (Table 2) across five LLMs convincingly demonstrates near-zero exposure of CRAFT versus substantial exposure of prior benchmarks, directly supporting the paper's core motivation

Comprehensive experimental coverage: six representative editing methods spanning parametric, retrieval-based, and alignment-based families, plus ablations of each KEDAS component and additional evaluation on four traditional benchmarks (Appendix G)

Reproducibility is well supported: hyperparameters, alignment-data construction, filter training details, prompts, example instances, and license information are all provided, and the data pipeline is claimed to be fully open-source
The paper is honest about limitations (Chinese-only, 2-hop composite reasoning, single LLM) and clearly delineates KEDAS from LTE and EREN
weaknesses: Main experiments use only one LLM (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct), so conclusions about both the benchmark's difficulty and KEDAS's superiority rest on a single model and cannot establish generality

Potential circularity between the benchmark and the method: KEDAS's alignment data, filter training data, and even the diverse edit augmentation forms (declarative/aliased) are explicitly designed around CRAFT's structure and training split, which weakens claims that KEDAS is a general-purpose paradigm; the paper itself concedes the augmentations are 'specifically designed for the CRAFT dataset'

The KEDAS components are relatively incremental: LoRA alignment with retrieved-edit prompts follows LTE, the self-adaptive routing resembles WISE's router and EREN's relevance check, and diverse augmentation is template-based paraphrasing; near-perfect locality scores (100.00) raise questions about whether the filter effectively memorizes the small test distribution (500 instances per subset)

The evaluation's meaning is limited by the domain: most edits are numeric values and composite reasoning requires arithmetic (e.g., computing a debt ratio of 0.5 or an M2 difference), so baseline failures on composite portability may reflect numeric computation rather than knowledge editing; exact-match on long decimals is a brittle metric

The exposure-rate measurement methodology is not described (how was 'known to the LLM' operationalized?), and the benchmark's 'real-time' claim sits awkwardly with the fixed released version used in all experiments
The benchmark covers only Chinese and two narrow domains with periodic updates, limiting immediate community impact despite the argument that the pipeline is language-agnostic

Some results are hard to interpret: EREN beating KEDAS on temporal locality is attributed to filter false negatives, but no error analysis or statistical significance testing is provided for the main comparisons

strengths: The motivation is clear and well-grounded: static knowledge editing benchmarks suffer from data contamination, and the exposure-rate analysis (Table 2) across five LLMs is a genuinely useful and concrete way to demonstrate this problem; CRAFT's near-zero exposure rates directly support the real-time/real-world claims.

The benchmark design is thoughtful in its evaluation dimensions: composite reasoning portability over paired edits, alias portability, temporal locality, and common-sense locality go beyond the standard ES/locality/portability triad and probe failure modes that prior benchmarks do not.

The 'easily-updated' data pipeline (official statistics and financial APIs) is a practical contribution, and the paper provides scripts so others can regenerate the benchmark for arbitrary time periods.

Experiments are reasonably comprehensive: seven editing methods are compared under a sequential-editing setting, ablations cover all three KEDAS components, and Appendix G shows KEDAS is also competitive on traditional benchmarks (ZsRE, WikiBio, WikiData), which guards against the method being CRAFT-specific.

Reproducibility is addressed explicitly: hyperparameters, prompts, filter training data construction, hardware, and runtimes are all reported, and the paper claims full open-source release of code and data.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty in KEDAS: it is largely an assembly of existing components (LTE-style alignment with LoRA, retrieval-based memory as in IKE/EREN, and a router deciding between edited and unedited paths, which closely mirrors WISE's side-memory router). The framing as a 'novel paradigm' overstates the contribution.

The ablation table undercuts the claimed contribution: w/o FLT and w/o SPI produce nearly identical results (e.g., 5.44 vs 5.68 on L_temporal), suggesting the 'self-adaptive post-alignment inference' adds little beyond the filter itself. This indicates the two headline components are largely redundant, and the paper does not analyze or explain this overlap.

The composite reasoning portability tests are confounded by arithmetic: answers like debt ratio = liabilities/assets are derivable by formula from the two retrieved edits, so high scores may reflect numeric computation after retrieval rather than genuine multi-edit knowledge integration. No analysis (e.g., decomposing errors, comparing against a trivial retrieve-and-compute baseline) is provided to rule this out.

Evaluation of the proposed method uses only a single model (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct), despite the exposure analysis spanning five LLMs; generality of KEDAS is therefore unverified, and no significance testing or variance reporting is provided for any main results.

The benchmark is narrow in scope: Chinese-language only, two domains (Chinese national statistics and Chinese listed-company finance), and composite reasoning is only 2-hop. These limitations are acknowledged, but they materially restrict the benchmark's reach as a general real-time editing benchmark; the 'alias' notion is also quite narrow (essentially swapping indicator names for English official terms).

Some results invite scrutiny rather than confidence: KEDAS achieves exactly 100.00 locality on both subsets while being outperformed by EREN on temporal locality, and its alias portability gains over IKE/LTE are modest (62.17 vs 60.98 for LTE on Finance), which weakens the 'significantly outperforms' narrative; explanations are given only post hoc (filter false negatives).

The exposure-rate methodology is not described in enough detail to verify (how exposure is measured, thresholds, whether generation or likelihood-based probing is used), which is problematic since it underpins the central claim about existing benchmarks' contamination.

Presentation issues: the repository URL is missing from the abstract, duplicate references appear (Cohen et al. 2024a/2024b are the same paper), and Table 1's tick/cross comparison is somewhat self-serving given that MQuAKE already supports composite multi-edit reasoning.

The benchmark's claimed 'ever-evolving' property is asserted but not demonstrated empirically: no experiment shows that regenerating the benchmark at a later date yields comparable difficulty or that the pipeline is robust to source-format changes.

strengths: CRAFT addresses a genuine gap: existing knowledge-editing benchmarks are static and suffer from contamination. The exposure-rate study across five LLMs (Table 2) provides concrete evidence that CRAFT knowledge is nearly unseen (0-1.8%) while prior benchmarks are substantially memorized, directly substantiating the real-time claim.

The benchmark design is thoughtful: paired edits enabling composite reasoning portability (integrating two distinct edits, e.g., assets + liabilities -> debt ratio), alias portability, and temporal/common-sense locality give a more comprehensive evaluation than prior datasets, and Table 1 positions it clearly against related work.

The data pipeline is built on officially updated public sources (NBS statistics, Eastmoney finance) with open scripts, so the 'ever-evolving' property is operationally credible rather than aspirational, unlike EvoWiki whose pipeline is unpublished.

The evaluation is reasonably broad: six representative editing methods spanning parametric, retrieval-based, and alignment-based paradigms, an ablation of all three KEDAS components (Table 6), and additional validation on four traditional KnowEdit benchmarks (Table 9) showing KEDAS generalizes beyond CRAFT.

Reproducibility is well supported: hyperparameters, alignment data construction, filter training data, augmentation prompts (with in-context examples), compute budget, deterministic decoding, and license documentation are all provided.
weaknesses: Potential benchmark-method circularity: KEDAS's near-perfect locality (100.00 on both L metrics) is largely an artifact of the self-adaptive routing rather than of editing itself - the ablation shows locality collapses from 100.0 to ~5.4 without the filter. Since CRAFT's temporal/indicator structure makes relevant-vs-irrelevant classification relatively easy for a trained BERT filter, the benchmark may partially measure retrieval relevance classification rather than knowledge editing, which inflates the headline claim that previous methods 'hardly achieve balanced performance.'

Only one LLM (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) is used for the main editing experiments, despite the exposure study covering five models. Conclusions about CRAFT's difficulty and KEDAS's superiority rest on a single model; the Limitations section acknowledges this but it weakens the empirical case for a main-conference paper.

The benchmark is Chinese-only and restricted to statistics/finance domains, limiting immediate community impact; the composite reasoning is only 2-hop. These scope restrictions are acknowledged but reduce the generality of the claimed contribution.

Methodological novelty of KEDAS is moderate: it is essentially LTE-style LoRA alignment plus a WISE-like routing decision plus retrieval augmentation with manually designed (declarative/aliased) edit forms. The augmentation types are explicitly tailored to CRAFT's format, so gains may not transfer to benchmarks with different edit structures without redesign.

The alignment/training data for KEDAS include composite portability QA pairs in the same format as the test metric, so P_reasoning gains may partly reflect format familiarity rather than genuine multi-edit integration; the paper does not disentangle this.

Some key details are underspecified or absent: the procedure for measuring exposure rates is not described, no significance testing or variance estimates are reported for the 500-instance-per-subset test sets, and the code/data URL in the abstract is blank in this version, which currently undermines the fully-open-source claim.

Minor presentation issues: duplicated Cohen et al. references (2024a/b), a few typos ('mapping an query', 'formularized'), and Table 1's characterization of prior benchmarks is somewhat self-serving (e.g., marking MQuAKE-CF as not real-world is debatable).

strengths: The paper addresses a real and well-motivated gap: existing knowledge editing benchmarks are static and suffer from data contamination. The exposure analysis (Table 2) is a valuable and unusual contribution, showing near-zero exposure for CRAFT versus 20-80% exposure for prior benchmarks, which substantiates the 'real-time' claim with evidence rather than assertion.

CRAFT is constructed from continuously updated official public APIs (NBS statistics, AShare), making the 'ever-evolving' property credible and practically sustainable; the pipeline and scripts are claimed to be open-sourced, supporting reproducibility.

The evaluation design is broader than prior datasets: composite reasoning portability over paired edits, alias portability, temporal and common-sense locality give a multi-dimensional view of editing quality beyond the usual ES/locality/portability triple.

Experiments are reasonably comprehensive: two domains, two LMs on CRAFT plus Llama-2-7B and Qwen2.5-7B on KnowEdit, seven baselines, both sequential and single editing settings, and an ablation (Table 7) that isolates the contribution of diverse edit augmentation, the filter, and self-adaptive inference.

The paper is candid about limitations (Chinese-only, 2-hop portability, dependence on the filter's robustness, limited baselines) and provides hyperparameters, prompts, and data statistics in appendices, which aids reproducibility.
weaknesses: There is a circularity concern: KEDAS's components (diverse edit augmentation forms, the filter training data, alignment data) are explicitly designed for CRAFT (the paper even states 'our augmentation methods are specifically designed for the CRAFT dataset'), and KEDAS is evaluated on CRAFT as the headline result. The near-perfect scores (ES ~100%, locality ~100%) partly reflect a filter that trivially routes irrelevant queries to the frozen model, so locality on CRAFT measures retrieval precision more than the edited model's behavior; the dataset may structurally favor the companion method.

The 'composite reasoning portability' is essentially 2-hop arithmetic (e.g., debt ratio = assets/liabilities), which is a narrow notion of reasoning; whether this meaningfully tests knowledge integration beyond simple calculation is under-argued.

Exposure analysis covers only five LMs and uses direct prompting to elicit exact numeric values; failure to recall a precise statistic under prompting does not fully rule out partial memorization or contamination, and no alternative probing (e.g., paraphrases, cloze, log-prob analysis) is attempted.

Only two LMs are evaluated on the main CRAFT results, and the KEDAS advantage on Qwen2.5 for alias portability is mixed (58.59 vs LTE's 58.92 on Statistics; some second-place finishes are glossed over). No significance testing or variance reporting is provided.

The temporal locality metric is under-explained: for real-time data the base model likely never knew any time period's value, so a change in behavior across neighboring periods may reflect general numerical-answer sensitivity rather than editing-induced temporal confusion.

Some claims are weakly supported: the explanation for KEDAS's imperfect L_temporal on Finance ('limited generalization of the BERT-based filter') is speculative; baseline exclusions (Appendix F) are justified mostly by engineering issues, which limits the completeness of the comparison.
The methodological novelty of KEDAS is modest, combining ideas from EREN (relevance filtering) and LTE (alignment); the paper acknowledges this, but the individual components are incremental.

strengths: The motivation for a continuously updatable, real-world, real-time knowledge editing benchmark is well-founded, and the identification of the contamination/staleness problem in existing datasets (ZsRE, MQuAKE, RippleEdits, WikiBigEdit, EvoWiki) is convincing and well-argued with Table 1 and the exposure analysis in Table 2.

The CRAFT dataset construction is grounded in official, continuously updated public data sources (NBS of China, annual financial reports) with an automated pipeline, which makes the 'easily-updated' claim plausible and gives the resource lasting practical value.

The proposed evaluation dimensions (composite reasoning portability over paired edits, alias portability, temporal and common-sense locality) go beyond standard single-edit ripple-effect tests and are a genuinely useful addition to how editing systems are stress-tested.

The paper is largely reproducible: code and data are stated to be released, hyperparameters, prompts, alignment data construction (Appendix A–D), compute budget, and licenses are documented, and experiments are run on an accessible single A40 GPU.

Evaluation coverage is reasonably broad: two CRAFT subsets, KnowEdit (four datasets), two LM families for CRAFT plus Llama-2-7B/Qwen2.5-7B in the appendix, sequential and single editing settings, and an ablation of the three KEDAS components (Table 7).
weaknesses: Evaluation circularity is the central weakness: KEDAS's augmentation templates, filter (bert-base-chinese), and retrieval are all explicitly designed for and trained on CRAFT's training split, and then the headline results are reported on CRAFT's test split. Near-100% edit success and 100% locality (Table 5) largely reflect the filter correctly routing test-distribution queries to the frozen model or to the adapter — a supervised routing problem the method was trained to solve — rather than genuine editing capability. The ablation confirms this: removing the filter or self-adaptive inference collapses locality to ~5–11%, so the 'editing' is mostly done by the classifier, not by the model.

The correctness metric for numeric answers is under-specified and possibly brittle. CRAFT answers are long exact numeric strings (e.g., 3033060.78); the paper never explains how answer correctness is judged (exact string match? tolerance? normalized?). For a benchmark paper whose main claim is fair evaluation, this is a serious omission that undermines confidence in all CRAFT results.

Novelty of KEDAS is limited and self-acknowledged: it borrows retrieval-with-relevance-decision from EREN and alignment-with-edit-prompt from LTE, adding augmentation forms (declarative/aliased) and the self-adaptive routing. The component pieces are straightforward, and the paper's own discussion (§4.5) concedes the derivation.

The exposure analysis is a crude proxy for contamination: directly prompting five LMs and counting correct answers conflates prior knowledge, guessing, and reasoning ability with memorization; GPT-3.5 answering 43.98% of ZsRE questions does not necessarily mean 'leakage' in a meaningful sense. The headline 'nearly 0% exposure' claim rests on this weak methodology.

Locality evaluation design is questionable: temporal-locality queries ask about neighboring years whose answers the model likely never knew (how is 'unchanged answer' judged when the base answer is wrong?), and common-sense locality uses C3 multiple-choice reading-comprehension questions, a format so different from the edited QA that near-perfect locality may be trivially attainable by any method that simply doesn't interfere.

Several baseline exclusions (MEMIT OOM, AlphaEdit, MEND, SERAC, RECIPE omitted from main CRAFT results on resource/compatibility grounds, Appendix F) weaken the empirical comparison, and no variance, seeds, or significance testing are reported for any main result, despite the gaps between methods being a key claim.

The generalization of KEDAS beyond the dataset it was designed for is untested in a meaningful way: KnowEdit results (Table 6) improve locality but portability is mixed (e.g., below WISE on WikiData_recent), and the method requires a retrained filter and re-tuned augmentation for each new domain, which limits the claimed 'paradigm' framing.

Scope is narrow: Chinese only, two domains (national statistics and finance), and composite reasoning limited to 2-hop pairs; the limitations section acknowledges these but the framing overstates the generality of the contribution.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and timely problem: knowledge editing benchmarks are largely static and suffer from data contamination, and the exposure analysis (Table 2) provides concrete evidence that existing benchmarks are substantially leaked while CRAFT is nearly contamination-free due to its real-time collection from official statistical/financial data sources.

CRAFT is well-motivated as an ever-evolving, automatically updatable dataset with a sustainable data pipeline (official APIs), and it introduces reasonable new evaluation dimensions (composite reasoning portability, alias portability, temporal/common-sense locality) that go beyond existing benchmarks like WikiBigEdit and EvoWiki.

The evaluation is relatively comprehensive: multiple representative editing paradigms (LoRA, ROME, IKE, EREN, WISE, LTE) across two LMs on CRAFT, plus validation on KnowEdit with additional LMs (Appendix I) and a single-editing setting, which supports the claim that KEDAS generalizes beyond the dataset it was designed for.

Ablation study (Table 7) isolates the contributions of diverse edit augmentation, the filter-based retriever, and self-adaptive post-alignment inference, and the components show interpretable effects on recall vs. locality.
Reproducibility appears strong: hyperparameters, prompts, filter training data construction, hardware details, and licenses are documented, and code/data are stated to be publicly released.
weaknesses: There is a risk that CRAFT and KEDAS are co-adapted: the dataset consists of exact numeric answers with structured edit pairs, which inherently favors a retrieval-based method with a relevance filter, while penalizing parametric methods (ROME, WISE). The near-ceiling results (ES ~100, locality 100) suggest KEDAS largely reduces to 'retrieve and read the edit,' and the paper does not adequately discuss whether this constitutes knowledge editing or retrieval-augmented generation, nor whether the benchmark fairly measures parametric editing capability.

The exposure analysis methodology is thin: it prompts five LMs once with each question and counts correct answers. A zero exposure rate for CRAFT is partly trivial (facts post-date model cutoffs) and single-prompt sampling is a weak probe of memorization; more rigorous probing (e.g., paraphrase sets, log-likelihood checks) would strengthen the contamination claim.

The ablation table contains a suspicious anomaly: 'w/o FLT' and 'w/o SPI' produce identical or near-identical results on CRAFT-Finance, which raises questions about whether the filter and the self-adaptive inference are actually measuring distinct mechanisms, or whether there is an experimental/reporting error. The paper's own discussion (§4.5) admits the ideas are borrowed from EREN and LTE, so the novelty of KEDAS is largely in their combination.

Locality of 100% for KEDAS invites the concern that the BERT-based filter simply learns to reject all out-of-scope queries by memorizing the training distribution; the paper offers no analysis of filter generalization (e.g., to unseen alias forms or unseen indicator types), even though the authors themselves note the filter may 'suffer from limited generalization' on L_temporal.

Evaluation details for numeric answers are under-specified: it is unclear how exact numeric targets are scored (exact string match vs. tolerance), which matters greatly for a benchmark built on statistics/finance values, and how answer formatting variations are handled for different models.

Coverage is limited to Chinese and two domains (national statistics, finance), and several modern baselines (MEMIT variants, MEND, SERAC, RECHE) were excluded from the main CRAFT experiments due to compatibility/resource issues, weakening the claim that 'previous methods hardly achieve balanced performance' on CRAFT.

There is an apparent inconsistency between Table 1 and the text: the table marks CRAFT's CRP column while the paper presents composite reasoning portability as a core novel feature of CRAFT; the RP/CRP definitions and markings should be reconciled.

Portability evaluation is limited to 2-hop arithmetic compositions over edit pairs, which is a narrow operationalization of composite reasoning; the limitation is acknowledged but restricts the benchmark's claimed comprehensiveness.
